paras: The lynching of Jack Betts took place at Corinth, Mississippi, early on the morning of August 13, 1900, when a mob of about fifty masked men took Betts, a Black farm laborer, from the county jail and hanged him to a telegraph pole. Betts had been jailed the day before, accused of assaulting a ten-year-old white girl. A brief wire report carried the killing to papers across the country, while the local weekly gave a long account that endorsed it.

Betts had come to Corinth from "[Boone]ville or somewhere in Prentiss" and had been hired as a laborer on the farm of Vernon Murphree, four miles east of the city. According to the Weekly Corinthian, which gave the family's version as fact, the Murphrees were awakened early on Sunday, August 12, by cries from their daughter's room, and Mrs. Murphree touched and recognized a man there. Murphree said he caught the man as he jumped to the ground, lost him in a short struggle, and, the night being clear and bright, identified him as Betts.

The neighborhood and the officers were notified and a search began, and about 8 o'clock that morning Betts was found in a house south of the foundry and placed in jail. The Corinthian wrote that the lynching that followed "was antici[pated] and expected."

The mob formed on the college hill about midnight and, after "mapping out the program," marched in twos to the jail, which it reached about 1 o'clock. Sheriff Wilson, on guard there, pleaded with the men "to let the law take its course" but gave way, the paper said, because further resistance would have meant the doors being battered in and other prisoners escaping. A large crowd of bystanders gathered, but the masked men let no one approach. Betts was dragged to a pole and hanged; before he died he "plead innocent of the crime and mumbled a great many prayers."

The body was cut down at daylight and a coroner's inquest was held, though no finding is reported. Betts's father came up from Booneville and took the body back there. The Corinthian said the news "caused no astonishment" and that there had been "no excitement about the matter," and no report of arrests, a grand jury or a trial appears in the coverage.

Most white papers ran a three-sentence Corinth dispatch on August 13 and 14, under headlines such as "Hanged to a Telegraph Pole" and "Negro Lynched at Corinth, Miss.," saying Betts "is said to have assaulted" or was "charged with assaulting" the girl. A Memphis-datelined version dropped the hedge: the Keowee Courier printed that he "committed" the assault, the Louisville Courier-Journal that he "criminally assaulted" the girl, and the San Antonio Daily Light that he was lynched "for rape." Weekly digests later reduced the story to one line, and one, in the Passaic City Record, had Betts taken "from the sheriff" and hanged "to a tree in the court house yard."

The Weekly Corinthian headlined a "Fiendish Assault," called Betts "the fiend" and "a burly negro," and closed by saying that "Southern communities when confronted with extreme cases, recognize but one law." On the same page it remarked that the St. Louis Chronicle's Corinth correspondent "might have made a stagger at the truth" in his report of the lynching, without saying what he had gotten wrong.

The only Black-press report found, in the American Citizen of August 17, reprinted the Corinth wire word for word under "HANGED TO A TELEGRAPH POLE," without comment. It ran directly after an item headed "UNUSUAL FOR GEORGIA," reporting that a Black man charged with assault at Marietta had been convicted and sentenced in court.

Accounts differ on where Betts was hanged: Filmore street near the railway crossing in the local paper's text, "near the public square" in its own headline, on the public square in the wire, and a court house yard tree in one digest; Memphis-datelined wires also gave the hour as 2 o'clock, against the local 1 o'clock. The local report, written in Corinth the same day, is the most detailed, but it rests on the Murphree family's account of the assault, which Betts denied.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Betts
bases: A masked mob took Jack Betts from the Corinth jail and hanged him to a pole (A3, A14, A21).

A mob of about fifty masked men took Betts from jail over the sheriff's protest and hanged him (A14, A3). They acted on an accusation of assaulting a white child, and the local paper defended the killing as the 'one law' of 'Southern communities' (A14).
The local Weekly Corinthian (A14) and the Corinth and Memphis wire reports (A3, A16, A21) agree that Betts was taken from jail and hanged at Corinth early on August 13.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the short wire under headings such as 'Hanged to a Telegraph Pole' or 'Negro Lynched at Corinth, Miss.', with the assault 'said to have' happened or 'charged'.
The Weekly Corinthian headlined a 'Fiendish Assault', called Betts 'the fiend' and wrote that Southern communities 'recognize but one law'.
Some Memphis-datelined versions dropped the hedge: 'committed an a sault', 'criminally assaulted', 'for rape'.
The American Citizen ran the wire verbatim under 'HANGED TO A TELEGRAPH POLE', directly after a Georgia item headed 'UNUSUAL FOR GEORGIA' about a Black man tried and sentenced in court; no comment.
